overview: The atlas calls this layer “Hadramaut” and marks it as a state from about 1000 to 1715. Its own borders tell a messier story. The 1000 polygon joins Wadi Hadramawt to Mahra and Dhofar; by 1492 it reaches deep into southern Oman; in 1530 it suddenly contracts to a Hadramawt core. Real history contained ports, valley towns, tribes, learned families and changing local dynasties, sometimes under wider Ayyubid or Rasulid claims. The ancient Kingdom of Hadramawt had ended centuries earlier, so it is not this state reborn. Sharma’s excavated warehouses held pottery and goods arriving from China, India, the Gulf and East Africa. Al-Shihr exported fish, incense and ambergris. Farmers directed rare floodwater across fields, while builders repeatedly repaired tall mudbrick homes. Shibam’s famous sanitation was clever: house shafts separated waste, and dried material helped fertilize gardens, an entire city partly organized around toilets! Families, merchants, craftspeople, herders, scholars and enslaved people did not share equal power. Tarim became a center of Arabic learning, but surviving chronicles favor prominent men and genealogies, so ordinary women and children are harder to see. The map’s 1715 disappearance records an atlas category change, not the end of Hadramawt or its people.

periods.title: Ports, valley towns and an atlas border already too large
periods.summary: The first exact polygon joins Hadramawt, Mahra and Dhofar but excludes tested Qana, which the atlas assigns to Yemen. Coastal ports and inland valley towns followed different local histories and economies. No single documented ruler matches the whole oversized shape.

periods.title: Sharma wanes while local powers and ocean routes change
periods.summary: The map holds the same broad outline. Archaeology dates Sharma’s end within this period; al-Shihr remains important, and evidence for the twelfth century is fragmentary. Ayyubid forces entered parts of Hadramawt late in the century, but town-level power stayed complicated.

periods.title: Ayyubid withdrawal, Rasulid expansion and separate Dhofar politics
periods.summary: Local families regained or retained towns after Ayyubid rule ended. Rasulid authority reached Hadramawt from 1229 through tribute, campaigns and delegated administration; Dhofar had its own Habudi phase. The atlas still erases these distinctions inside one state-colored polygon.

periods.title: Rasulid claims, local rulers and an expanded map
periods.summary: The 1279 polygon expands and absorbs Qana and southern-Oman points. Rasulid rulers defeated Habudi Dhofar and claimed a wider sultanate, yet local dynasties and tribal powers remained. A destructive 1348 flood near Tarim shows environmental events crossed political labels.

periods.title: Rasulid decline, Tahirid competition and Kathiri growth
periods.summary: The atlas retains a broad southern-Arabian unit while Rasulid power weakened and ended in 1454. Tahirid and Kathiri ambitions overlapped with local town rulers. Chroniclers’ genealogies served legitimacy, so reconstructing a neat succession is less secure than the map’s solid color suggests.

periods.title: A giant polygon is an atlas expansion, not a sudden empire
periods.summary: The exact border jumps east and north across much of southern Oman, reaching nearly 60 degrees east. No cited political history supports one Hadrami state matching that footprint in 1492. Kathiri-Mahra rivalry and Dhofar’s history must remain distinct from the map’s editorial sweep.

periods.title: Badr Abu Tuwayriq, Sayun and Portuguese coastal violence
periods.summary: The huge map continues while Kathiri ruler Badr Abu Tuwayriq made Sayun’s palace a residence in 1519. Portuguese force struck Indian Ocean shipping and al-Shihr’s coast. These events involved a regional ruler and port communities; they did not create control over every place inside the polygon.

periods.title: The atlas finally separates a Hadramawt core from Mahra and Oman
periods.summary: At 1530 the target contracts sharply. Tested Qishn, al-Ghaydah and Dhofar points move to Mahra, while Oman-interior points move to Gharra or Oman layers. Kathiri power remained important, but ports, tribes and towns continued to negotiate authority rather than forming one centralized bureaucracy.

periods.title: Local rule, archives and Tarim’s scholarly networks
periods.summary: The contracted polygon stays stable across three exact intervals. A surviving Kathiri archive begins in 1622, and Tarim scholar Abdallah al-Haddad lived from 1634. Such documents reveal real institutions and learning, yet they illuminate particular families and places rather than everyone inside the border.

periods.title: Mukalla’s al-Kassadi emirate and an editorial endpoint
periods.summary: Mukalla’s separate al-Kassadi emirate began in 1703 while the atlas still shows one Hadramaut layer. In 1715 the id vanishes, but no successor polygon automatically owns audited Wadi and coastal cities. The disappearance therefore cannot be narrated as one conquest or the fall of Hadramawt.

items.text: The indexed record says “Hadramaut,” state, circa 1000 to 1715, but its twelve border files do not trace one verifiable government. The coverage is continuous as map data; political unity is not. This card therefore treats the id as an editorial territorial umbrella whose contents change.

The imported paragraph stretches Hadramawt across modern Hadramawt, Shabwah, Mahra, Dhofar and beyond. A scholarly regional reference instead distinguishes a stricter wadi-centered meaning from broad geographical usage. A modern administrative list cannot be projected backward as a medieval border or government.

Ancient Hadramawt was a kingdom centered on Shabwa and connected to Qana, but it ended around the third century CE. Medieval Arabic writers later used Hadramawt geographically. Calling the atlas’s 1000 layer that ancient kingdom revived would skip roughly seven centuries and invent continuity.

At 1492 the polygon includes Hadramawt cities, Dhofar, Mahra and tested points as far east as Mahout in Oman. In 1530 those eastern places split among Mahra, Gharra and Oman layers. That crisp switch exposes cartographic classification, not a surveyed frontier changing overnight.

Historians face another warning: medieval Hadrami documentation is scarce, and surviving accounts can promote genealogy or clan honor. Archaeology, architecture and archives help check chronicles, but none makes ordinary lives fully visible. Uncertainty here is historical honesty, not an empty space to fill with legend.

sections.title: Wadis, coast, desert and precious water

items.text: Hadramawt combines a deeply cut inland wadi system, high limestone plateaus, desert margins and an Arabian Sea coast. Communities at Tarim or Shibam faced different water, travel and work from fishers at al-Shihr. The atlas color hides those ecological differences inside one shape.

Rain could be rare yet violent. Farmers guided short-lived floodwater with banks, dikes and channels, gaining water and fresh sediment while risking fields and houses. “Spate irrigation” means catching a rush, not turning the wadi into a permanently flowing river.

Water management was also social. Studies of Wadi Sana connect runoff and landforms with water rights, territory and cooperation. A channel reveals engineering, but its repair required decisions about labor and shares. Environmental need alone cannot tell us who controlled the gate or received water first.

A historical study records a 1348 flood that destroyed palms and about twenty mosques around Tarim. Floods could nourish agriculture and suddenly wreck it, so resilient settlement required rebuilding. Dates in chronicles are valuable, though one recorded disaster cannot stand for every valley or century.

The early atlas border absorbs monsoon-influenced Dhofar, but al-Balid’s archaeology shows its own rulers and commercial history. Mahra surveys likewise identify separate ports east of al-Shihr. Geography connected these regions; it did not make their political histories, communities or economies interchangeable.

Tarim, Shibam, al-Shihr, Sayun and Mukalla were not five offices of one timeless capital. Sources name different ruling families and phases, including Rashidids, Ayyubid intervention, Rasulid claims, Tahirid competition and Kathiri expansion. Control could mean tribute, a governor, a garrison or temporary submission.

Rasulid rule linked Hadramawt to a larger Yemeni sultanate from the thirteenth through fifteenth centuries, yet local families sometimes governed on its behalf. Even Rasulid origin stories were reworked to claim South Arabian legitimacy. A dynasty’s genealogy was political argument as well as family history.

Mukalla offers a useful local timeline: a small port is recorded in 1035, al-Muzaffar fortified it in 1271, and an al-Kassadi emirate began in 1703. Those dates show urban and political change without making Mukalla the capital of the entire atlas polygon throughout.

Sayun Palace became Badr Abu Tuwayriq’s residence in 1519. Its ventilation shaft, rainwater drainage, mudbrick, timber and lime record craft as clearly as rulership. Later additions mean the present seven-story building cannot be treated as an unchanged photograph of the palace in 1519.

The 1715 map does not hand Mukalla, Shibam, Tarim, Sayun or al-Shihr to a single successor id. Hadramawt’s places and institutions continued, including separate local powers. The atlas endpoint is therefore a deletion in this dataset, not a documented state-wide surrender or cultural ending.

sections.title: Ports, crafts and an ocean of exchange

items.text: Sharma was a specialized, fortified entrepôt active roughly 980 to 1180. Excavators found warehouses and goods moving through an Indian Ocean web; about seventy percent of pottery was imported from regions stretching from China to East Africa. A busy cargo stop was not necessarily a large family city.

Al-Shihr’s evidence mixes texts with a carefully excavated tell. Sources describe dried and large fish, incense, ambergris and fine camels; Indian pots held or cooked foods and liquids. Because excavation covered only part of the oldest quarter, absence elsewhere is not proof a craft or food was missing.

Surveyors recorded 174 sites along the Hadramawt to Mahra coast and identified several active ports of about the ninth to twelfth centuries. That distribution replaces the idea of one lonely harbor. Coastal communities could compete, specialize, decline or continue on different schedules.

Mukalla’s seaside buildings later combined residence and storage for merchants and fishers linked with Africa and India. The nomination also describes much later Indian-influenced architecture, which this card does not back-project. Trade contact was old; every visible palace façade is not medieval.

Merchants and scholars traveled through Aden, the Hejaz, Dhofar, India and farther shores, but “Hadrami network” did not mean every resident went overseas. Farmers, builders, herders, servants and children made local lives possible while a smaller number of travelers connected distant households and markets.

sections.title: Food came from fields, herds, sea and trade

items.text: Spate-water fields and palms supported valley settlements, while sheep and camels used drier country. Medieval Yemen-wide agricultural writings discuss wheat, sorghum, dates, grapes, cotton and many other plants, but a Rasulid handbook is not a Hadramawt grocery receipt. Local proof must remain local.

Fish mattered especially on the coast. Al-Shihr redistributed large and dried fish toward Oman, Aden and Basra; some dried catch even fed animals. Inland households had different access, so the port’s famous products should not become a single daily menu for every Wadi family.

Archaeologists found imported cooking and storage pots associated with water, milk and foods at al-Shihr. Those ceramics came through ocean trade. Pots prove containers and connections more securely than recipes; nobody can reconstruct one “Hadrami dinner” from a shard alone.

Rasulid court records show lavish redistribution and food allotments to royal women and enslaved people. That is evidence of hierarchy and palace supply, not ordinary abundance. A ruler’s kitchen could display imported wealth while rural or urban workers faced very different portions and seasonal risks.

Wadi Daw’an is renowned today for honey, palms, farming and herding, and UNESCO presents these as long-lived traditions. Medieval beekeeping is plausible within that continuity, but the detailed modern landscape is later comparison. The safest fun fact remains that honey connects flowers, skilled hive care and trade.

sections.title: Mud homes, clothing, work and moments of fun

items.text: Shibam’s dense tower houses used sun-dried mudbrick and rose above a floodplain inside defensive walls. The surviving urban ensemble is chiefly sixteenth century, with older mosque and castle elements. Families repeatedly replastered earthen walls, so maintenance was skilled work, not a sign that mud was primitive.

Wadi Daw’an builders mixed mud, straw and palm material and used stone, palm trunks and sidr wood. Villages perched on slopes or outcrops above cultivated ground. UNESCO describes living continuity; individual medieval houses still require dating rather than assuming every traditional technique stayed unchanged.

House plans organized storage, privacy, ventilation, work and waste vertically. Sayun Palace’s central shaft moved light and air, while Shibam’s towers reduced exposed ground area. Architecture gives clues to movement through rooms, yet it rarely tells which child slept where or who told bedtime jokes.

Textiles, leather and metal were promoted in Rasulid Yemen, and port trade moved cloth and other goods, but this record lacks a securely dated Hadramawt wardrobe. Clothing varied by wealth, work, gender and town. Illustrated later dress should not become a medieval uniform for everyone in the polygon.

We know people gathered for worship, markets, weddings, visits and seasonal work, but surviving sources preserve elite genealogies and disputes better than games or humor. A kid-readable card can admit that laughter surely happened while refusing to invent a favorite toy, punch line or festival rule.

sections.title: Families, women, children and social rank

items.text: Kin groups and family reputation could shape protection, marriage, office, property and conflict. Shibam’s dense defenses partly answered rivalry among prominent families. That evidence does not make every household a feuding clan: neighbors also had to cooperate on walls, water, streets and fields.

Chronicles often foreground sada lineages, scholars and rulers, which makes genealogy look like all of society. Knysh shows those pedigrees can carry agendas. Craftspeople, fishers, farmers, herders, servants and enslaved people remain less individually named, though their labor supported towns and elite institutions.

Women appear in court allotments, kin histories and later Hadrami ethnography, but direct 1000 to 1715 evidence for ordinary women is uneven. It would be reckless to assign all weaving, farming or childcare to one gender. Tasks changed with place, status, wealth, age and household need.

Children learned language, prayer, manners and practical skills within households and workplaces; some studied reading and religious texts with teachers. Tarim’s scholarly reputation documents institutions more clearly than enrollment. We cannot assume every boy attended or that girls never learned from literate relatives.

Slavery was part of medieval Yemeni society, with enslaved people recorded as soldiers, cooks, concubines, quarry workers, merchandise, salary recipients and even officials. Those different lives shared legal unfreedom, not one experience. Evidence for Hadramawt specifically is scattered, so regional examples are labeled as such.

sections.title: Learning, belief, books and a local Arabic sample

items.text: Hadramawt became strongly associated with Shafi‘i law and Sufi teaching, but neither spread in one simple wave. Historians must compare biographies, genealogies and institutional claims because later writers could magnify a founder or lineage. Religious history was lived locally and remembered competitively.

Tarim’s mosques, retreats and learning centers made it an important scholarly town. The famous al-Mihdar Mosque originated in the fifteenth century, though its striking present minaret and many palace influences are later. Buildings can preserve long learning traditions while changing form repeatedly.

Libraries in Tarim, Aynat and Mukalla preserve Arabic historical, legal, religious and medical manuscripts. Catalogs reveal what survived, not what every family read. Copy dates can be later than composition, damaged volumes lose context, and private collections make the surviving sample selective.

A Kathiri document archive begins in 1622, offering firmer evidence for administration, transactions and named actors near the end of this card. Paper archives are major achievements of record keeping, yet survival favors institutions and property disputes more than children’s conversations or workers’ jokes.

Local written-language sample: رسالة المعاونة والمظاهرة والمؤازرة, Risālat al-muʿāwanah wa-l-muẓāharah wa-l-muʾāzarah, “The Treatise of Assistance, Support, and Aid.” Tarim scholar ʿAbdallāh al-Ḥaddād composed this Arabic work in 1069 AH, or 1658 to 59 CE, securely inside the mapped interval. One author’s title does not speak for everyone.

sections.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question

items.text: Fifteenth-century scholar Baḥraq al-Hadrami wrote a didactic work on Galenic medicine. His career shows medical knowledge could circulate through scholars even where trained physicians were scarce. A learned text records recommended ideas; it cannot prove how every sick villager was diagnosed or treated.

A fourteenth-century Rasulid travel guide advised on thirst, hunger, fatigue, weather, illness, foods and medicinal plants. It illuminates knowledge available in Yemen’s learned world, especially to travelers, but it is not a field notebook from every Hadramawt household or proof each remedy worked.

Care also happened without formal doctors: relatives could bring water, food, rest and company, while religious teachers encouraged visiting sick people. These acts are historically plausible and partly textually visible, but archaeology rarely preserves a bowl beside a patient with a label saying who cared.

Shibam’s heritage system separated liquid and solid waste through house shafts and outlets. Dried solids could fertilize nearby gardens, linking toilets, agriculture and mudbrick production. The funny truth is technically serious: town planning partly followed poo. Dating each installation still requires building-level study.

No single toilet arrangement is proven for every town or all seven centuries. Water installations, flood channels, wells and waste paths needed maintenance, while contaminated water and crowding could spread illness even without germ theory. The evidence is strongest at Shibam and must stay there.

Walls, hilltop villages, towers and forts reveal insecurity as well as prestige. Shibam’s compact houses offered refuge during family rivalry, while Sayun Palace began as a defensive fortress. Fortification never guarantees constant war; it records preparation, authority and the value placed on protected homes and stores.

Portuguese expansion brought armed coercion to the Indian Ocean and violence at al-Shihr in the early sixteenth century. Hadrami chronicles are crucial but must be read beside other records. A raid affected sailors, merchants and families; it was not merely a colorful meeting of cultures.

Local rulers, tribal forces, townspeople, religious mediators and outside dynasties bargained, fought and collected revenue. Wider states could claim tribute without managing every alley or field. Treating power as layered better explains why the atlas border can coexist with several named political actors.

Major achievements were cooperative and cumulative: directing floods, maintaining fields, building and replastering tall earthen homes, operating ports, navigating sea routes, copying books and sustaining teaching networks. None belongs to one dynasty alone, and much depended on workers whose names the chronicles omitted.

At 1715 the exact map layer ends, but Hadramawt does not. Local institutions, valley towns, scholarship, farming and maritime connections continued in changing forms. The honest ending is political and cartographic continuity: no invented fall, extinction, successor state or frozen modern border.

ending.text: The exact atlas id disappears in 1715, but the border snapshot assigns no single successor to audited Mukalla, Shibam, Tarim, Sayun or al-Shihr points. Hadramawt’s towns, local powers, farms, ports, archives and scholarly communities continued through new political arrangements. Because the layer had already merged and then separated Hadramawt, Mahra, Dhofar and southern Oman, its disappearance is best read as a taxonomy change rather than one state’s conquest, a people’s migration or a cultural ending.
